Indian Standard
METHOD FOR DETERMINATION OF LINEAR DENSITY OF TEXTILE FIBRES ( GRAVIMETRIC METHOD)

( First Revision)
.O. FOREWORD
0.1 This Indian Standard ( First Revision ) was adopted by the Indian Standards Institution on 26 March 1973, after the draft finalized by the Physical Methods of Test Sectional Committee had been approved by the Textile Division Council. 0.2 This standard was first published in 1952 which prescribed the use of some patented instruments for the measurement of linear density ( mean fibre weight per unit length ) of cotton fibre. .This standard has been revised to cover many other textile fibres also and to accommodate the developments which have taken place since the publication of this Reference to patented instruments has been dropped to standard. accommodate other instruments available for the purpose. Opportunity has also been taken to align the standard with IS0 Recommendation R-1973 * Determination of linear density of textile fibres - Gravimetric Assistance has also been drawn from ASTM. Designation: Method'. D 1769-1967 `Method of test for linear density of cotton fibres ( array sample)' issued by American Society for Testing and Materials. 0.3 In reporting the result of a test made in accordance with this standard, if the final value, observed or calculated, is to be rounded off, it shall be done in accordance with IS : 2-1960*.

1. SCOPE Ll This standard prescribes two methods for determination of linear density of textile fibres. One method is applicable to cut fibre bundles and the other to whole fibres. 1.1.1 Both the methods given are applicable only for discrete fibres (excluding fibres like jute ) which can be kept straight and parallel
*Rules for rounding off numerical values ( rauircd ).

3

ISt234-1973
during the preparation of bundles. They arc not applicable to fibres having pronounced crimp ( such as Indian wools ). 2. PRINCIPLE tuft having known number of fibres is cut in the 2.1 Method I -A middle to a known length and the mass of the cut-middle portion is From the mass and total length of fibres the linear density determined. is calculated. 2.2 Method lI - Fibres which have been sorted previously into groups of known length are weighed and then counted. Then the mass per unit length is calculated from the number, mass and length of fibres. 3. TERMINOLOGY 3.0 For the purpose of this standard, (see also IS : 232-1967; ). following definitions shall apply

3.1 Linear Density - Mass per unit length; the quotient obtained by dividing the mass of the fibre by its length. It is expressed in millitex or decitex. 3.2 ArraySorted fibres placed in order of length. CONDITIONS FOR CONDITlONlNG AND

4. ATMOSPHERIC TESTING

4.1 The test sample shall be conditioned as laid down in IS: 6359-1971t and test carried out in the standard atmospheric conditions of 65 f 2 pacent relative humidity and 27 f 2�C temperature. 5. SAMPLING 5.1 The test samples of fibres shall be so selected as to be the representatives of the lot. The samples drawn in accordance with the procedure laid down in the material specification or in compliance with an agreement between the buyer and the seller shall be held to be the representative of the lot. Norx - In case of cottonfibrc rdercnce to IS : 4952-19623 be made. 6.

Is:23401973 6.2 The gross sample approximately 1 kg shall be spread out evenly on a level ground in the form of either a square with each side slightly greater than 1 m or in the case of a larger sample, a rectangle with the 1 m and the larger side slightly shorter side slightly greater than greater than 2 m. Over this, a metallic framework of size 1 x 1 m with 25 sub-squares or 1 x 2 m with 50 sub-squares, as the case may be, From each of these sub-squares one bunch ( or more ) of shall be placed. taking care (a) not to exercise any fibres shall be pulled out at random, bias in favour of or against any particular place within a sub-square, and (b) that the fibres drawn from each sub-square weigh about the same The total quantity of about 5 to 10 g of fibres drawn shall amount. constitute the reduced sample. 6.3 The reduced sample shall be divided into 25 or 50 approximately equal groups. From a different portion of each of these groups, one small tuft ( or more ) of fibres shall be extracted at random, taking care that the fibres drawn are nearly equal in weight, and the total weight of fibres thus This shall constitute the ` test sample `. drawn is not less than 200 mg. 7. TESTING 7.1 After pre-conditioning, bring the sample to constant mass in standard atmosphere. 8.2.2 Cut the middle part of each combed tufi to a given length ( as great as possible ) under the minimum tension necessary to remove crimp, Take the necessary precautions so that by means of the cutting device. there are no free fibre -ends anywhere except at the two ends of the cut tufts. 8.2.3 Place the ten tufts so obtained on the velvet board and cover them with the glass plate from the edge of which they should protrude slightly. 8.2.4 From each of the ten tufts in turn, take out sufficient number of fibres, so as to form a tuft, weighing about @2 mg, in each case drawing the fibres from one cut end. Make sufficient number of tufts, so that a iota1 number of at least 1 000 fibres in the case of natural fibres and 200 fibres in the case of man-made fibres are covered. Condition these tufts in the standard atmosphere and then- weigh them individually, using the balance to an accuracy of 0.02 mg. 8.3 Calculations- Calculate the linear density of the fibres by dividing mass by the total length of cut fibres in the each tuft. Then determine the mean linear density for all the tufts from the values obtained for each tuft. 9.
